transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today, and what would you like help with?

I’ve been feeling really overwhelmed and not coping well with some recent stress in my life. It’s starting to affect how I function day to day, and I’m hoping to understand what’s going on and how to handle it better.
Did these difficulties start clearly after a specific stressful event or change in your life, and if so, about how long after that did you begin to feel this way?
Yeah, it really started after I was laid off from my job about five months ago. I began feeling this way maybe two or three weeks after that, and it’s been going on pretty steadily since then.
Day to day, do you feel more persistently sad and lose interest or pleasure in things, or is it more that you feel tense, on edge, and constantly worried about many things even when you try to relax?

It’s really a mix of both for me. I feel down and uninterested in things I used to enjoy, but at the same time I’m constantly on edge and worrying about money and what’s going to happen next, even when I’m just sitting at home trying to relax.

Over the past two weeks, have you had most days where you felt sad or down nearly all day and also lost interest or pleasure in almost all activities, or are there still many moments when you can enjoy things if the stress about your job and money eases up a bit?

Over the past two weeks I’ve felt low and worried most days, but it’s not quite all day, every day. I can still enjoy things a bit at times—like getting into a TV show or laughing with a friend—but as soon I start thinking about work or money again, the heaviness and anxiety come right back.

Over the last six months, have you found yourself worrying about many different areas of your life on most days and feeling physically tense or restless, even when nothing specific is happening in that moment, or do the worries mainly come up when you’re directly thinking about your job and money situation?

It’s mostly when I’m thinking about my job situation and money that I get really wound up and tense. When I’m distracted or with friends and not focused on that stuff, the anxiety eases up a fair bit, though it never feels completely gone.

How much have these feelings and worries been interfering with your daily life—for example, your sleep, concentration, relationships, or ability to job hunt or manage daily tasks—and do you feel they’re more intense or long‑lasting than what people around you in a similar situation seem to experience?

They’re getting in the way quite a bit—my sleep is lighter and more broken, I have trouble focusing when I try to work on applications, and some days I just can’t get myself to do basic chores. I’ve also been pulling back from friends because I feel drained. It does feel like I’m taking this harder and for longer than a few others I know who’ve lost jobs around the same time.
With how low and overwhelmed you’ve been feeling, have you had any thoughts that life isn’t worth living, that you’d be better off dead, or any thoughts about harming yourself in any way?

I have had some passing thoughts like “what’s the point” or that it wouldn’t matter if I didn’t wake up, but I haven’t made any plans or tried to hurt myself. Those thoughts come and go, usually when I’m really stressed about money, but they’re not constant.

If your job and money situation were suddenly resolved tomorrow, do you feel that your mood and energy would mostly return to normal fairly quickly, or do you sense that this low, heavy feeling has taken on a life of its own and would likely continue anyway?

I think if the job and money stuff were suddenly sorted, a lot of this would lift pretty quickly. I can imagine feeling more like myself again within a week or two, though I’d probably still be a bit shaken and cautious for a while.

Aside from feeling distressed, do you still feel basically like yourself in terms of your personality and ability to cope, or do you feel as if this experience has fundamentally changed who you are or how you function most of the time?

I still feel mostly like myself underneath all of this, but it’s like my usual coping just isn’t working as well. I’m more withdrawn and easily overwhelmed than I used to be, but I don’t feel fundamentally like a different person.

Since losing your job, have you started doing anything to cope that feels clearly unhealthy or out of character for you—like drinking more, using drugs, overspending, or avoiding important responsibilities most of the time?

Yeah, I have, a bit. I’ve been drinking more in the evenings than I used to and putting off things I know I should be doing, like job applications and dealing with bills, sometimes for days. It’s not constant, but it’s definitely more than was normal for me before all this.

latest_inference.note: Previously the only candidate was an adjustment-related condition. The current interview continues to support this and does not introduce clear evidence for other syndromes. Symptoms began within a few weeks after a clearly identifiable psychosocial stressor (job loss), have persisted for several months, and consist of mixed depressive and anxiety features plus some maladaptive coping (increased drinking, avoidance). The distress is experienced as clearly linked to the stressor, with the patient believing mood would largely normalize if the situation improved, and they still feel essentially like themselves. The symptom pattern does not meet the threshold for a more severe, autonomous mood or anxiety disorder (e.g., the low mood is not nearly all day every day, enjoyment is still possible, worries are focused mainly on the stressor rather than generalized across domains). There is some passive death ideation but no plan or intent, which can occur in this context and does not in itself necessitate adding a separate mood disorder diagnosis. No evidence has emerged for psychosis, substance dependence, bipolarity, or primary anxiety disorders. Therefore the candidate list remains the same with one stress-related diagnosis and no additions or removals.

opening_question.question: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today, and what would you like help with?

final_diagnosis.reason: Symptoms began within a few weeks of a clearly identifiable psychosocial stressor (job loss), have persisted for about five months, and consist of mixed depressive and anxious symptoms that are distressing and cause functional impairment but do not meet full criteria for a major depressive episode or generalized anxiety disorder. The patient reports partial preservation of enjoyment, mood closely tied to the stressor, and a belief that symptoms would largely resolve if the stressor improved, all consistent with an adjustment disorder rather than an independent mood or anxiety disorder.
